newsitem.title: USA: US Justice official to Brussels for Boeing talks.
newsitem.headline: US Justice official to Brussels for Boeing talks.

text.p: The U.S. Justice Department's top antitrust official will travel to Brussels in the next few days to discuss the Boeing -McDonnell Douglas merger, now nearing a critical vote by the European Union, sources said on Wednesday.

The Justice Department said acting antitrust division chief Joel Klein will travel to Brussels very soon. Those familiar with the purpose of his visit said he would be discussing the Boeing deal with his counterparts at the EU.
With only two weeks left until a vote on the merger, European officials are pondering whether to clear the deal, as the United States Federal Trade Commission did earlier this month.

There is strong sentiment in Europe against the merger because of fears that if the two American producers of large commercial airplanes combine they would have an unfair edge over the European consortium, Airbus Industrie.
On the other hand, some commentators have asserted there could be a trade war if the Europeans exercise their authority to block the deal.
It is against this background the Europeans are reaching out to consult with American trade and competition officials.

Low level European trade officials are to meet on Thursday and Friday in Washington with the U.S. Trade Representative's office. They will discuss a 1992 agreement which was supposed to limit government subsidies -- both direct and indirect -- to commercial airplane makers.
EU officials have said the 1992 deal has failed sufficiently to limit indirect U.S. subsidies, provided in defense contracts to firms which also produce civilian aircraft.
The low level trade talks are regularly scheduled under the 1992 agreement. Europeans have unsuccessfully pressed for a renegotiation of the 1992 treaty.

The talks with the Justice Department's Klein are under a separate 1991 agreement which provides for consultation between the competition authorities in Europe and the United States on matters of "national concern."
The choice of Klein appears to indicate a desire by the EU to negotiate directly with representatives of President Bill Clinton.
In the United States, antitrust jurisdiction is shared between Klein's antitrust division and the Federal Trade Commission, an independent, bipartisan agency.
The independent FTC made the Boeing decision, but Klein -- like the U.S. Trade Representative's office -- works in the executive branch for President Clinton.
In addition, the FTC has made clear its view that there is no antitrust problem with the merger.

Bill Baer, a top FTC official who oversaw the investigation of the merger, said on Wednesday his review showed that Douglas aircraft was "in sort of a death spiral" and too weak to compete for commercial aircraft sales.

Nonetheless, Baer said he had read news reports that EU officials have suggested to Boeing and McDonnell Douglas they take "six months or so in which an effort is made to find an alternative buyer for Douglas Aircraft, to see if there could be a buyer out there."
In Brussels, a Boeing executive told Reuters that EU competition authorities had made no such demands on Boeing, but said the concern had been raised.
"This has not been a demand of the European Commission, it's been something which has been raised," the executive said.
"We know there is an area of concern which is the size of the in-service fleet (of McDonnell Douglas). We are working on remedies to address those concerns," the executive said.
